claim: PtdIns4P gradients between organelle membranes and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are thought to drive counter-transport of other lipids via non-vesicular traffic.
source: Gradients of PtdIns4P between organelle membranes and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are thought to drive counter-transport of other lipids via non-vesicular traffic.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this model, as indicated in the abstract and introduction sections.

claim: The phosphoinositide-motive force pathway requires SAC1 phosphatase to degrade PtdIns4P in a 'cis' configuration at the ER to maintain the gradient.
source: This novel pathway requires the SAC1 phosphatase to degrade PtdIns4P in a 'cis' configuration at the ER to maintain the gradient.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement stated in the abstract based on the proposed model.

claim: SAC1 has been proposed to act in 'trans' at membrane contact sites, which could oppose lipid traffic.
source: However, SAC1 has also been proposed to act in 'trans' at membrane contact sites, which could oppose lipid traffic.
evidence: This claim references prior proposals in the literature about SAC1's mode of action.

claim: Acute inhibition of SAC1 causes accumulation of PtdIns4P in the ER.
source: We report that acute inhibition of SAC1 causes accumulation of PtdIns4P in the ER
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: SAC1 does not enrich at membrane contact sites.
source: that SAC1 does not enrich at membrane contact sites
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: SAC1 has little activity in 'trans', unless a linker is added between its ER-anchored and catalytic domains.
source: and that SAC1 has little activity in 'trans', unless a linker is added between its ER-anchored and catalytic domains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: PtdIns4P is a crucial metabolic intermediate in the synthesis of plasma membrane inositol lipids PtdIns(4,5)P2, PtdInsP3 and PtdIns(3,4)P2.
source: Firstly, PtdIns4P is a crucial metabolic intermediate in the synthesis of the plasma membrane inositol lipids PtdIns(4,5)P2, PtdInsP3 and PtdIns(3,4)P2 (Brockerhoff and Ballou, 1962; Stephens et al., 1991; Posor et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PtdIns4P binds to and thereby recruits and/or activates many proteins involved in cellular traffic.
source: Secondly, PtdIns4P binds to and thereby recruits and/or activates many proteins involved in cellular traffic (Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PtdIns4P is synthesized by two families of PI 4-kinases.
source: PtdIns4P is synthesized by two families of PI 4-kinases, each with their own unique modes of regulation (Boura and Nencka, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The primary route of PtdIns4P catabolism is via removal of the 4-phosphate by SAC family lipid phosphatases.
source: The primary route of the lipid's catabolism is via removal of the 4-phosphate by SAC family lipid phosphatases (Balla, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The principle enzyme for PtdIns4P catabolism in budding yeast is the highly conserved SAC1 enzyme.
source: The principle enzyme in budding yeast is the highly conserved SAC1 enzyme (Guo et al., 1999; Rivas et al., 1999; Hughes et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SAC1 is an integral membrane protein with two C-terminal transmembrane helices.
source: SAC1 is an integral membrane protein with two C-terminal transmembrane helices (Whitters et al., 1993; Konrad et al., 2002; Nemoto et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: SAC1 localizes primarily to the ER but is also able to traffic to the Golgi depending on the growth status of the cell.
source: which localizes primarily to the ER but is also able to traffic to the Golgi depending on the growth status of the cell (Faulhammer et al., 2007; Blagoveshchenskaya et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ER makes extensive membrane contact sites with the Golgi, PM and endosomes.
source: but the realization that the ER makes extensive membrane contact sites (MCS) with all of these organelles
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The crystal structure of SAC1 revealed an approximately 70 amino acid region between the N-terminal catalytic domain and C-terminal transmembrane domains that was disordered in the crystal.
source: Indeed, the crystal structure of SAC1 revealed an approximately 70 amino acid region between the N-terminal catalytic domain and C-terminal transmembrane domains that was disordered in the crystal
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies.

claim: The disordered stretch in SAC1 was proposed to be able to span the 15–20 nm gap between ER and organelle at MCS and confer 'trans' activity.
source: this stretch was proposed to be able to span the 15–20 nm gap between ER and organelle at MCS and confer 'trans' activity (Manford et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a prior hypothesis cited from the literature.

claim: Targeting of SAC1 to ER-PM MCS by the Osh3 protein was proposed to allow dephosphorylation of PM PtdIns4P by cortical ER-localized SAC1 in 'trans'.
source: Subsequently, targeting of SAC1 to ER-PM MCS by the Osh3 protein was proposed to allow dephosphorylation of PM PtdIns4P by cortical ER-localized SAC1 in 'trans', hence controlling plasma membrane inositol lipid synthesis and function (Stefan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a prior hypothesis cited from the literature.

claim: Dynamic localization of SAC1 to ER-PM MCS has been proposed to regulate PM inositol lipid function in mammalian cells.
source: More recently, dynamic localization of SAC1 to ER-PM MCS has been proposed to regulate PM inositol lipid function in mammalian cells (Dickson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a prior hypothesis cited from the literature.

claim: Synthesis of PtdIns4P on cellular membranes can be used to drive counter-transport of other lipids against their concentration gradients.
source: The picture is complicated by a recently proposed novel mode of action for PtdIns4P: that its synthesis on cellular membranes can be used to drive counter-transport of other lipids against their concentration gradients (de Saint-Jean et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a model proposed in prior research.

claim: OSBP-related lipid transfer proteins operating at MCS collect their lipid cargoes from the ER and transfer them to the destination membrane.
source: In this model, oxysterol binding protein (OSBP)-related lipid transfer proteins operating at MCS collect their lipid cargoes from the ER (where they are synthesized) and transfer them to the destination membrane (such as the PM or Golgi).
evidence: This describes a model from prior research.

claim: The lipid transfer domain preferentially collects and back-traffics a PtdIns4P molecule instead of the cargo lipid to avoid futile reverse transfer.
source: The lipid transfer domain then avoids a futile reverse transfer reaction because it preferentially collects and back-traffics a PtdIns4P molecule instead.
evidence: This describes a mechanism from the proposed model.

claim: Futile traffic of PtdIns4P from the ER back to the destination membrane is prevented because the PtdIns4P is degraded by ER-localized SAC1 acting in 'cis' configuration.
source: Crucially, futile traffic of PtdIns4P from the ER back to the destination membrane is prevented because the PtdIns4P is degraded by ER-localized SAC1, acting in this case in a 'cis' configuration.
evidence: This describes a key requirement of the proposed model.

claim: The energy of ATP hydrolysis by PI4K during PtdIns4P synthesis is harnessed to build and maintain a steep chemical gradient of PtdIns4P at the destination membrane with respect to the ER.
source: Ultimately, the energy of ATP hydrolysis by PI4K during PtdIns4P synthesis is harnessed to build and maintain a steep chemical gradient of PtdIns4P at the destination membrane with respect to the ER.
evidence: This describes the energetics of the proposed model.

claim: Flow of PtdIns4P down its concentration gradient via OSBPs powers counter-transport of other lipids against their own chemical gradients.
source: Flow of PtdIns4P down this concentration gradient via OSBPs thus powers counter-transport of other lipids against their own chemical gradients.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the proposed model.

claim: Direct evidence for PPInMF-driven transfer reactions have been presented at the trans-Golgi network for sterols.
source: Direct evidence for PPInMF-driven transfer reactions have now been presented at the trans-Golgi network (TGN) for sterols (Mesmin et al., 2013; von Filseck et al., 2015b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Direct evidence for PPInMF-driven transfer reactions have been presented at the PM for phosphatidylserine.
source: and at the PM for phosphatidylserine (Moser von Filseck et al., 2015a; Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: A critical requirement for the PPInMF is that SAC1 acts in a 'cis' configuration in the ER.
source: A critical requirement for the PPInMF is that SAC1 acts in a 'cis' configuration in the ER
evidence: This is a logical requirement of the model.

claim: 'Trans' activity of SAC1 would act to dissipate the PtdIns4P gradients at MCS and make counter-transport much less efficient.
source: 'trans' activity would act to dissipate the PtdIns4P gradients at MCS and make counter-transport much less efficient.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model.

claim: In vitro experiments have demonstrated that SAC1 can act in the required 'cis' configuration.
source: In vitro experiments have demonstrated that SAC1 can indeed act in the required 'cis' configuration (Mesmin et al., 2013; von Filseck et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Loss of SAC1 'trans' activity would cause accumulation of PtdIns4P in membranes like the PM and Golgi where the lipid is synthesized.
source: Loss of SAC1 'trans' activity would cause accumulation of its PtdIns4P substrate in membranes like the PM and Golgi where the lipid is synthesized
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model, also shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Loss of SAC1 'cis' activity predicts accumulation of PtdIns4P in the ER.
source: whereas loss of 'cis' activity predicts accumulation of PtdIns4P in the ER (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae with deletions of their Sac1 gene show 6–10 fold increases in PtdIns4P mass.
source: Saccharomyces cerevisiae with deletions of their Sac1 gene show 6–10 fold increases in PtdIns4P mass (Rivas et al., 1999; Hughes et al., 2000; Guo et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies in yeast.

claim: In yeast Sac1 deletions, PtdIns4P has been reported at both the PM and the ER, depending on the probe used.
source: with PtdIns4P reported at both the PM (Roy and Levine, 2004; Stefan et al., 2011) and the ER (Roy and Levine, 2004; Tahirovic et al., 2005; Cai et al., 2014), depending on the probe used.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: RNAi of SAC1 in mammalian cells causes 1–2 fold accumulation of PtdIns4P.
source: RNAi of SAC1 in mammalian cells causes 1–2 fold accumulation of PtdIns4P (Cheong et al., 2010; Dickson et al., 2016; Goto et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: RNAi of SAC1 in mammalian cells results in PtdIns4P accumulation in the ER.
source: with accumulation reported in the ER (Cheong et al., 2010; Blagoveshchenskaya et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Acute knock-out of SAC1 in HeLa cells with CRISPR/Cas9 was reported to induce PtdIns4P accumulation on the PM and endosomes.
source: On the other hand, acute knock-out of SAC1 in HeLa cells with CRISPR/Cas9 was reported to induce PtdIns4P accumulation on the PM and endosomes (Dong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The SACM1L gene is essential to the survival of single mammalian cells.
source: However, these experiments are hard to interpret, since the SACM1L gene is essential to the survival of single mammalian cells (Blomen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: SAC1 is a member of an especially redox-sensitive family of lipid phosphatases.
source: As a member of an especially redox-sensitive family of lipid phosphatases
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAC1's biochemical properties.

claim: SAC1 is inherently sensitive to inhibition by oxidizing compounds including bis-peroxovanadates (bpVs) and hydrogen peroxide.
source: SAC1 is inherently sensitive to inhibition by oxidizing compounds including bis-peroxovanadates (bpVs) and hydrogen peroxide (Rosivatz et al., 2006; Ross et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Treatment of cells with 500 µM peroxide induces a massive 7-fold accumulation of PtdIns4P in mammalian cells.
source: In fact, treatment of cells with 500 µM peroxide was shown to induce a massive 7-fold accumulation of PtdIns4P in mammalian cells (Ross et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Over-expressed soluble SAC1∆TMD in COS-7 cells greatly reduced PM localization of P4M, indicating PtdIns4P was depleted.
source: SAC1∆TMD expression in COS-7 cells greatly reduced PM localization of P4M, indicating PtdIns4P was depleted
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A catalytically inactive C389S mutant of SAC1∆TMD had no effect on PM PtdIns4P levels.
source: whereas a catalytically inactive C389S mutant was without effect (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Acute treatment of cells over-expressing SAC1∆TMD with 500 µM peroxide led to a rapid (<1 min) recovery of PM PtdIns4P.
source: Acute treatment of these cells with 500 µM peroxide led to a rapid (<1 min) recovery of PM PtdIns4P
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with 10 µM bpV(HOpic) caused a slower recovery of PM PtdIns4P over approximately 5 min in cells over-expressing SAC1∆TMD.
source: treatment with 10 µM bpV(HOpic) caused a somewhat slower recovery of PM PtdIns4P over approximately 5 min (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Over-expressed SAC1∆TMD can be inhibited in the context of a living cell by peroxide and bpV(HOpic).
source: Clearly, the over-expressed SAC1∆TMD could be inhibited in the context of a living cell.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: Under the experimental conditions used, ER-PM MCS marked with GFP-ORP5 were unaffected by peroxide treatment.
source: However, under our experimental conditions, ER-PM MCS marked with GFP-ORP5 (that would be responsible for PtdIns4P traffic) were unaffected by peroxide treatment (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Treatment with peroxide stimulated a rapid (commencing within 5 min) accumulation of ER PtdIns4P.
source: Cells were treated with peroxide or bpV(HOpic) for one hour, which stimulated a rapid (commencing within 5 min) accumulation of ER PtdIns4P with peroxide
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Treatment with bpV(HOpic) caused a slower, but robust accumulation of PtdIns4P in the ER.
source: and a slower, but robust accumulation in the ER with bpV(HOpic) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ER localization of the accumulated PtdIns4P pool was verified by co-expression with iRFP-tagged Sec61β.
source: ER localization of the accumulated PtdIns4P pool was verified by co-expression with iRFP-tagged Sec61β (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A similar accumulation of ER-signal was observed with a second, high affinity PtdIns4P biosensor GFP-P4C.
source: We observed a similar accumulation of ER-signal with a second, high affinity PtdIns4P biosensor GFP-P4C (Weber et al., 2014) as shown in Figure 1G.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Upon acute inhibition of SAC1, transfer of PtdIns4P to the ER continues, but SAC1 is unable to dephosphorylate it, leading to massive accumulation of the lipid in the ER.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for these data is that upon acute inhibition of SAC1, transfer of PtdIns4P to the ER continues, but SAC1 is unable to dephosphorylate it, leading to massive accumulation of the lipid in this compartment (Ross et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data with citation to prior work.

claim: Most proteins known to function at MCS are enriched at them.
source: Although this is not inconsistent with the firmly established localization of SAC1 throughout the ER (Rohde et al., 2003; Nemoto et al., 2000), most proteins known to function at MCS are enriched at them too (Gatta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A HEK-293A cell line was engineered to stably over-express GFP1-10.
source: We then edited these cells to introduce the GFP11 tag to the N-termini of either the SAC1 protein, the ER-resident Sec61β or the MCS protein Extended Synaptotagmin 1, E-Syt1 (Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is described in the methods and results sections.

claim: The 293AGFP1-10 cells were edited to introduce the GFP11 tag to the N-termini of SAC1, Sec61β, and E-Syt1.
source: We then edited these cells to introduce the GFP11 tag to the N-termini of either the SAC1 protein, the ER-resident Sec61β or the MCS protein Extended Synaptotagmin 1, E-Syt1 (Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is described in the methods and results sections.

claim: Genotyping of edited cells produced the predicted 200 bp amplicon in the edited cells but not in the un-edited 293AGFP1-10 cells.
source: In each case, the predicted 200 bp amplicon was produced in the edited cells but not in the un-edited 293AGFP1-10 cells (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sanger sequencing of amplicons spanning the edited site verified insertion of the GFP11 tag in frame.
source: Sanger sequencing of amplicons spanning the edited site in each case was accomplished with GFP11 primers to verify insertion of the tag in frame.
evidence: This is described in the results section.

claim: GFP11-SAC1 in edited cells showed the expected ER/Golgi localization.
source: Confocal imaging revealed the expected ER/Golgi localization of GFP11-SAC1 in edited cells, showing co-localization with the ER marker VAPB and the cis/medial Golgi marker Mannosidase II (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GFP11-E-Syt1 and GFP11-Sec61β revealed exclusively ER localization in medial confocal optical sections.
source: Medial confocal optical sections of GFP11-E-Syt1 and GFP-11-Sec61β also revealed exclusively ER localization (Figure 2C), consistent with previous reports (Saheki et al., 2016; Leonetti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and citations to prior work.

claim: GFP11-SAC1 exhibited a reticular distribution by TIRF microscopy.
source: Like GFP11-Sec61β, GFP11-SAC1 exhibited a reticular distribution
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GFP11-SAC1 showed juxta-nuclear enrichment likely corresponding to the bottom of the Golgi.
source: though unlike Sec61β, it also showed juxta-nuclear enrichment likely corresponding to the bottom of the Golgi (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GFP11-E-Syt1 revealed a reticular distribution by TIRF with numerous bright puncta that are most likely ER-PM MCS.
source: GFP11-E-Syt1 also revealed a reticular distribution by TIRF, but with numerous bright puncta that are most likely ER-PM MCS (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Quantitative analysis revealed no enrichment of GFP11-SAC1 close to the basal PM as compared to ER-localized GFP11-Sec61β.
source: Quantitative analysis of the ratio of fluorescence intensity via TIRF imaging (selective for signal within ~100 nm of the coverslip) vs conventional epi-illumination (exciting fluorescence throughout the entire volume of the cell) revealed no enrichment of GFP11-SAC1 close to the basal PM as compared to ER-localized GFP11-Sec61β
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GFP11-E-Syt1 showed a marked enrichment close to the basal PM compared to ER-localized proteins.
source: whereas GFP11-E-Syt1 showed a marked enrichment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Expressed SAC1 exhibits an identical localization to the endogenous protein.
source: To produce a more quantitative, rigorous comparison of MCS vs non-MCS localization of SAC1, we turned to expression of GFP-SAC1 in COS-7 cells, since expressed SAC1 exhibits an identical localization to the endogenous protein (Rohde et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GFP-SAC1 localizes to the total ER with a distribution indistinguishable from calreticulin or Sec61β.
source: As can be seen, GFP-SAC1 localizes to the total ER with a distribution indistinguishable from calreticulin or Sec61β
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Contact site proteins (ORP5, E-Syt2, MAPPER) exhibit punctate distributions coinciding with MAPPER.
source: whereas the contact site proteins all exhibit punctate distributions coinciding with MAPPER, although the association between MAPPER and E-Syt2 is not as tight as it is with ORP5 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In the resting state, SAC1 does not specifically localize at ER-PM MCS.
source: Collectively, these data show that, in the resting state, SAC1 does not specifically localize at ER-PM MCS.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: PLC induces the hydrolysis of PM PtdIns(4,5)P2 to produce the calcium-mobilizing messenger, InsP3.
source: PLC induces the hydrolysis of PM PtdIns(4,5)P2 to produce the calcium-mobilizing messenger, InsP3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PLC signaling.

claim: Calcium release from ER stores triggers transient recruitment of E-Syt1 to ER-PM MCS.
source: The resulting calcium release from ER stores triggers transient recruitment of E-Syt1 to ER-PM MCS (Giordano et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Calcium release leads to depletion of ER calcium, triggering aggregation of the ER calcium sensor STIM1 and its recruitment to ER-PM MCS to activate store-operated calcium entry.
source: Subsequently, calcium release leads to depletion of ER calcium, triggering aggregation of the ER calcium sensor STIM1 and its recruitment to ER-PM MCS to activate store-operated calcium entry across the PM (Liou et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Continued breakdown of PtdIns(4,5)P2 yields diacylglycerol, which is converted to phosphatidic acid and exchanged for ER-derived PtdIns by MCS-recruited Nir2.
source: Finally, the continued breakdown of PtdIns(4,5)P2 yields diacylglycerol, which is converted to phosphatidic acid and exchanged for ER-derived PtdIns by MCS-recruited Nir2, facilitating PtdIns(4,5)P2 replenishment (Chang et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Stimulation with 100 µM ATP triggered GFP-E-Syt1 to rapidly (peaking within 30 s) and transiently (returning to baseline within 2 min) recruit to punctate ER-PM MCS.
source: Stimulation of endogenous PLC-coupled P2Y receptors (Hughes et al., 2007) with 100 µM ATP triggered GFP-E-Syt1 to rapidly (peaking within 30 s) and transiently (returning to baseline within 2 min) recruit to punctate ER-PM MCS
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: STIM1 exhibited a slower (peaking within 2 min) transient recruitment to ER-PM MCS upon ATP stimulation.
source: whereas STIM1 exhibited a slower (peaking within 2 min) transient recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GFP-Nir2 exhibited a much slower (5 min) recruitment that was sustained during the 10 min experiment.
source: GFP-Nir2 exhibited a much slower (5 min) recruitment that was sustained during the 10 min experiment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GFP-SAC1 showed no change in its localization close to the PM upon ATP stimulation.
source: GFP-SAC1, on the other hand, showed no change in its localization close to the PM
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ER-resident proteins GFP-calreticulin and GFP-Sec61β showed no change in localization upon ATP stimulation.
source: nor did the ER-resident proteins GFP-calreticulin or GFP-Sec61β (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Carbachol elicited a typical, transient elevation of cytosolic calcium with a sustained plateau that was unchanged by tagging endogenous proteins with GFP11.
source: Carbachol elicited a typical, transient elevation of cytosolic calcium (measured with Fura-red) with a sustained plateau that was unchanged by tagging endogenous proteins with GFP11 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Carbachol stimulation caused the rapid, transient recruitment of GFP11-E-Syt1 to puncta.
source: Stimulation caused the rapid, transient recruitment of GFP11-E-Syt1 to puncta (Figure 3C), as seen previously with endogenously tagged GFP-E-Syt1 in HeLa cells (Saheki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and citation to prior work.

claim: No change in the localization of endogenous GFP11-SAC1 or GFP11-Sec61β was observed upon carbachol stimulation.
source: However, no change in the localization of endogenous GFP11-SAC1 or GFP11-Sec61β was observed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SAC1 is not specifically enriched at (nor depleted from) ER-PM MCS, even when other proteins are being recruited to these sites.
source: Together, these results show that SAC1 is not specifically enriched at (nor depleted from) ER-PM MCS, even when other proteins are being recruited to these sites to facilitate calcium and inositol lipid homeostasis.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The limited and unchanging localization of SAC1 at MCS appears co-incidental with its well-known distribution throughout the ER.
source: The limited and unchanging localization of SAC1 at MCS therefore appears co-incidental with its well-known distribution throughout the ER.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: PM-anchored FKBP and ER-anchored FRB can be induced to form ectopic ER-PM MCS using rapamycin.
source: PM-anchored FKBP and ER-anchored FRB can be induced to form ectopic ER-PM MCS using this system (Várnai et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GFP-P4M × 2 was able to detect residual PtdIns4P in the PM of SAC1∆TMD-FKBP over-expressing COS-7 cells.
source: This reporter was able to detect residual PtdIns4P in the PM of SAC1∆TMD-FKBP over-expressing COS-7 cells (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A fusion of FKBP to the N-terminus of SAC1 showed robust recruitment of the enzyme to ER-PM MCS within 1 min of rapamycin addition.
source: A fusion of FKBP to the N-terminus of SAC1 showed robust recruitment of the enzyme to ER-PM MCS within 1 min of rapamycin addition (see the inset graphs)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FKBP-SAC1 produced a very subtle decline of PM PtdIns4P as compared to the catalytically inactive C389S control, though this did not reach statistical significance.
source: and we detected a very subtle decline of PM PtdIns4P as compared to the catalytically inactive C389S control, though this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.15, Tukey's multiple comparison test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fusion of FKBP to the C-terminus of SAC1 produced a greater depletion of PtdIns4P relative to its C389S control.
source: Fusion of FKBP to the C-terminus of the protein produced a greater depletion of PtdIns4P relative to its C389S control (p=0.007)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SAC1∆TMD-FKBP expressed poorly in cells and recruited much less robustly than the 'trans' acting fusions of full-length SAC1.
source: This protein expressed poorly in cells, and recruited much less robustly than the 'trans' acting fusions of full-length SAC1
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: An order of magnitude less SAC1∆TMD-FKBP was recruited than full-length FKBP-SAC1 or SAC1-FKBP.
source: An order of magnitude less SAC1∆TMD-FKBP was recruited than full-length FKBP-SAC1 or SAC1-FKBP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Recruitment of SAC1∆TMD-FKBP was accomplished in <1 min, and the effect on PM PtdIns4P was much more dramatic than seen with either full-length fusion or the catalytically inactive C389S mutant.
source: Nevertheless, recruitment was still accomplished in <1 min, and the effect on PM PtdIns4P was much more dramatic than seen with either full-length fusion or the catalytically inactive C389S mutant of this construct (p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fusion of FKBP to the N-terminus of SAC1∆TMD produced better expression and more robust recruitment than the C-terminal fusion.
source: Fusion of FKBP to the N-terminus of SAC1∆TMD produced better expression and more robust recruitment than the C-terminal fusion
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FKBP-SAC1∆TMD produced a slightly more efficient depletion of PtdIns4P than SAC1∆TMD-FKBP.
source: and also a slightly more efficient depletion of PtdIns4P (p=0.0008)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ~70 amino acid region between the N-terminal catalytic domain and the TMD of SAC1 are essential for substrate recognition and catalysis.
source: It has previously been reported that the ~70 amino acid region between the N-terminal catalytic domain and the TMD of SAC1 are essential for substrate recognition and catalysis (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SAC1∆452-587-FKBP recruited to the PM robustly but failed to induce any PtdIns4P depletion.
